title: Elimination of the formation of biofilm in industrial pipes using enzyme cleaning technique
author: Liu, Tang, et al.

steps.title: Set temperature and pH
steps.instruction: Maintain the cleaning system at 45 ± 2 °C and adjust the water tank pH to 10 ± 1 before adding any reagents.

steps.title: Drain retention water
steps.instruction: Fully drain all retention water from the pipes and associated equipment.

steps.title: Remove in-line micro filter
steps.instruction: Remove any in‑line micro filter with nominal pore size < 50 µm unless it must remain to protect equipment or will be cleaned separately.

steps.title: Add soda to achieve pH
steps.instruction: Pump detergent 2 (soda) at 200 g L⁻¹ into the water tank until the tank pH is 10 ± 1.

steps.title: Add enzyme to reach concentration
steps.instruction: Pump detergent 1 (N‑acetylmuramide glycanohydrolase enzyme) into the water tank until the enzyme concentration reaches 0.25 % (w/v).

steps.title: Test enzyme concentration with Aller kit
steps.instruction: Verify enzyme concentration using the Aller test kit.

substeps.instruction: Collect 500 mL of the prepared enzyme solution.
Using a disposable syringe, transfer 5 mL of the solution into a clean flask (flask and syringe pre‑washed with the same solution).
Add two drops of Cl‑1 reagent; the solution should turn purple.
Add Cl‑2 reagent dropwise while shaking until the colour changes from purple to yellow.
Add Cl‑3 reagent dropwise while shaking until the colour changes from yellow back to purple; record the volume of Cl‑3 reagent consumed as V₁.
Repeat the above procedure with the initial water (no enzyme) and record the volume of Cl‑3 reagent consumed as V₀.
Calculate enzyme concentration using Ec = (V₁ − V₀) × 372; the result must be within 0.25 ± 0.02 %.

steps.title: Circulate enzyme solution through pipes
steps.instruction: Circulate the verified enzyme solution through all pipes and equipment that require cleaning.

description: In the water treatment process, traditional CIP techniques can usually remove or sterilize microbes on the surface of pipes. Taking the advantages of low cost and low energy consumption, these strategies were universally used in food, fermentation, and water treatment industry [1,3]. However, when the biofilm forms in pipelines, the traditional methods would not be available to eliminate it completely [2]. By contrast, the strategy of using muramidase to remove the biofilm in pipes is more effective and in-depth. The comparison of effectiveness between the traditional CIP and enzyme cleaning technique is shown in Fig. 1 and Table 1.
